content: Among target populations, tracking the distribution of HIV self-testing (HIVST) kits is essential for program managers to monitor progress and predict the need for supportive services. These services include linking clients to confirmatory testing and antiretroviral therapy (ART) as required, as well as ensuring the availability of commodities in the supply chain. The number of HIVST kits distributed should be recorded, rather than the number of individuals receiving them, to avoid double counting. Data should be collected at the lowest distribution point, such as the site or individual providing the kits to those self-testing. Reporting is recommended on a quarterly basis (every three months). Disaggregation of data should include gender (male, female, transgender), age groups (10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35–39, 40–44, 45–49, 50+), and key populations (e.g., men who have sex with men, people living in prisons or other closed settings, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals). In high-burden settings, additional priority populations such as adolescent girls and young women should also be included. The HIVST approach should align with national program specifications. The percentage of key population members who tested for HIV in the past 12 months or know their current HIV status is a critical indicator of progress in providing HIV testing services to these groups. Knowing one’s HIV status is essential for accessing care and treatment, living a healthy and productive life, and reducing the risk of HIV transmission. In many countries, focusing testing and counseling efforts on high-burden locations and populations is the most efficient way to reach people living with HIV and ensure they are aware of their status. The numerator for this indicator includes the number of respondents who know they are living with HIV or those who report having tested for HIV in the last 12 months and received a negative result. The denominator is the total number of respondents. Data collection methods include representative surveys of key populations, such as bio-behavioral surveys (BBS), behavioral surveillance surveys (BSS), or HIV sentinel surveillance (HSS+). Disaggregation should include gender, age (<25, 25+), and key populations. The number and percentage of people on ART among all people living with HIV at the end of the reporting period is a measure of treatment coverage and progress toward providing ART to all individuals living with HIV. This indicator is central to achieving the second 90/95 target: ensuring that 90% of people who know their HIV-positive status are accessing ART by 2020 and 95% by 2025. The numerator includes the number of people on ART at the end of the reporting period, while the denominator includes the estimated number of people living with HIV or those who know their HIV status. Retention and attrition analyses should be conducted to ensure accurate reporting, and the numerator should exclude individuals who have stopped treatment, died, or were lost to follow-up (LFU). The recommended threshold for defining LFU is 28 days after the last scheduled appointment, rather than the previous 90-day standard. The percentage of people living with HIV on ART for at least six months who achieve virological suppression (viral load <1000 copies/mL) is a key clinical outcome indicator. Viral load suppression (VLS) reflects the effectiveness of ART services and is the best available measure of patient adherence to treatment. The numerator includes individuals on ART for at least six months with at least one routine viral load test result showing suppression during the reporting period. The denominator includes all individuals on ART for at least six months with at least one routine viral load test result. Data sources include program records (e.g., ART registers, patient records, laboratory records) or population-based surveys. This indicator should be interpreted alongside viral load testing coverage to assess potential biases. The number of people living with HIV who initiated ART during the reporting period is an indicator of ART program expansion. Monitoring trends in new ART patients provides critical information for forecasting antiretroviral (ARV) needs and allocating staff to ensure quality care. ART initiation is also a sentinel event for case surveillance. The numerator includes individuals who initiated ART in accordance with national treatment guidelines during the reporting period. Disaggregation should include gender, age, key populations, and other priority groups such as pregnant or breastfeeding women and serodiscordant partners. The percentage of people living with HIV who initiate ART with a baseline CD4 count of <200 cells/mm³ measures the proportion of individuals with advanced HIV disease (AIDS) at the time of ART initiation. Late ART initiation is a risk factor for treatment failure and often reflects late diagnosis. The numerator includes individuals initiating ART during the reporting period with a baseline CD4 count of <200 cells/mm³, while the denominator includes all individuals initiating ART with a baseline CD4 count. Data sources include program records (e.g., ARV registers, laboratory records). Disaggregation should include gender, age, key populations, and other priority groups. In settings with robust electronic health information systems (HIS), monitoring mean and median CD4 counts among those initiating ART is recommended. Viral load testing coverage, defined as the percentage of people on ART for at least six months who have a viral load test result, is a critical measure of program performance. Routine viral load testing is recommended at six months after ART initiation, with a reporting window of 5–7 months. Disaggregation should include gender, age, and key populations. Additional or alternative disaggregations may be appropriate depending on HIS capacity.
